blindSummary:
This is a dangerous destination for trans visitors — and narrowly avoided becoming much worse. In February 2024 parliament unanimously passed an anti-LGBT "family values" bill: up to 3 years in prison for simply identifying as LGBT, and 5 years for "promotion." The president refused to assent pending legal challenges, the supreme court dismissed the challenges in December 2024, and the bill lapsed when parliament dissolved at the end of its term — but its unanimous passage and broad public support signal the political climate, and reintroduction is expected.

Under existing law, "unnatural carnal knowledge" carries up to 3 years, and mob justice against perceived LGBT people is documented. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection. The capital has a resilient underground community (one LGBT+ organisation's 2021 office opening was raided and shut down within weeks), but nothing that can protect a visitor.
blindOutOfScope: The 2024 bill never became law (lapsed unassented); its significance is climate/trajectory.

Public broadcaster (Dec 2024): this country's supreme court unanimously dismissed two legal challenges to the anti-LGBT bill (three years' imprisonment for identifying as LGBT, five for forming or funding LGBT groups), ruling the cases could not be reviewed until presidential assent. Same-sex activity was already punishable by up to three years. Fear and uncertainty gripped the country's LGBT community; the UN condemned the bill as one of the most draconian on the continent.

Legal news outlet (Feb 2024): this country's parliament unanimously passed the anti-LGBT 'family values' bill, criminalising identifying as LGBTQ+ (up to 3 years) and forming or funding LGBT groups (up to 5 years); the bill proscribes 'propaganda, advocacy or promotion' of LGBTQ+ activities.

International human-rights organisation report (Jan 2018), on the forced concealment of queer identity under this legal regime - full PDF: violence and discrimination against LGBT people in this country; a criminal-code provision criminalises 'unnatural carnal knowledge' but is rarely enforced; documents mob violence, police abuse, and extortion.

Rights-organisation report page (Jan 2018): opens with a first-person account - a lesbian woman beaten by a crowd and nearly burned in a major city after a police officer kicked her; this country criminalises same-sex conduct via a historic law that is rarely enforced, but unlike some neighbouring states has not stiffened penalties - documents pervasive violence and discrimination.

Bachelor's thesis (2017, produced at a university abroad): survey of 113 migrants from this country living abroad on LGBT rights at home - most opposed decriminalisation/legalisation, citing religio-cultural reasons and effects on children; most supported families loving and accepting LGBT members but not blessing their marriages.
blindTangential: “Unnatural carnal knowledge” (up to 3 years) criminalises same-sex conduct — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the lapsed bill would have criminalised identity itself.
